title: The Minimal Hypothesis: [CommRing R] [IsBezout R]
content:
The parent entry proved the GCD complete characterization for Euclidean domains and asked two questions: can it be stated for IsBezout instead, and what is the minimal typeclass? This entry answers both. The minimal hypothesis is a bare commutative Bézout ring: [CommRing R] [IsBezout R]. This is even weaker than a Bézout domain — no IsDomain axiom is required — and it drops the Euclidean division algorithm, Noetherianity, the PID structure, and DecidableEq/GCDMonoid all at once.

A Bézout ring is defined by: every finitely generated ideal is principal. Equivalently, every pair of elements has a linear-combination gcd.
mathContext: IsBezout R ⇔ every finitely generated ideal of R is principal ⇔ span{x,y} is principal for all x, y. Euclidean domains ⊊ PIDs ⊊ Bézout domains ⊊ Bézout rings.

title: Abstract gcd as an Ideal Generator
content:
The whole proof pivots on Mathlib's IsBezout.gcd a b, defined as a *generator of the principal ideal span{a,b}* — not via any Euclidean algorithm. Its universal property is packaged as gcd_dvd_left, gcd_dvd_right (it divides a and b) and dvd_gcd (any common divisor divides it).

gcd_dvd_linear_combination uses gcd_dvd_left/right to show gcd divides a·x + b·y. gcd_achievable_Bezout uses the ideal-theoretic Bézout witness IsBezout.gcd_eq_sum (∃ u v, u·a + v·b = gcd), reoriented by `ring` into the a·x + b·y convention.
mathContext: IsBezout.gcd a b := generator (span{a,b}). Since span{a,b} is principal (span_pair_isPrincipal instance from [IsBezout R]), the generator exists; it is unique only up to a unit, hence noncomputable.

title: The Characterization and Its Backward Direction
content: linear_combination_iff_gcd_dvd is the headline result: ∃ x y, a·x + b·y = c ↔ gcd(a,b) ∣ c. Forward is gcd_dvd_linear_combination. Backward: from gcd ∣ c obtain k with c = gcd·k; from gcd_eq_sum obtain u, v with u·a + v·b = gcd; then c = (u·a + v·b)·k = a·(k·u) + b·(k·v), closed by `ring` after rewriting. gcd_complete_characterization_Bezout then follows verbatim from the parent via simp_rw with the divisibility equivalence.
mathContext: The argument uses no Euclidean structure — only that gcd divides a, b and is a linear combination of them. This is exactly the content of IsBezout, which is why it is the minimal hypothesis.

title: Structural Essence and Coprimality
content:
span_pair_eq_span_gcd states span{a,b} = span{gcd(a,b)}: the ideal of all linear combinations of a and b is principal, generated by their gcd. This is the one-line heart of the whole story (it is IsBezout.span_gcd reversed) and is exactly the property that fails in a UFD like ℤ[X], where gcd(2,X)=1 but 1 ∉ span{2,X}.

isCoprime_iff_gcd_isUnit specializes the main equivalence at c = 1: a and b are coprime iff their gcd is a unit, via isUnit_iff_dvd_one.
mathContext: In ℤ[X]: span{2,X} = {2f + Xg} is the maximal ideal of polynomials with even constant term, which is NOT principal — so ℤ[X] is not Bézout, though it is a UFD. This is the precise boundary the IsBezout hypothesis draws.

title: One Statement, Many Rings
content: Three inferInstance examples locate the result in the algebraic hierarchy: every EuclideanDomain is Bézout (so this subsumes the parent), every IsPrincipalIdealRing is Bézout (and needs no IsDomain), and every ValuationRing is Bézout. The valuation-ring case is the genuinely new territory: valuation rings of non-discrete valuations are not Noetherian, hence not PIDs and not Euclidean domains, yet the characterization applies to them without change.
mathContext: Instance chain in Mathlib: EuclideanDomain → IsPrincipalIdealRing → IsBezout, and ValuationRing → IsBezout (Mathlib.RingTheory.Valuation.ValuationRing). A single [CommRing R] [IsBezout R] theorem therefore covers ℤ, ℚ[X], ℤ[i], all PIDs, and all valuation rings simultaneously.
